Otolaryngology · published research

Nasal polyposis

A 30-participant open study after sinus surgery reported smaller or fewer recurrent polyps and improved obstruction scores when mixed-spectrum rhinophototherapy was added to intranasal steroid. Its design does not isolate the light effect.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 30-participant open study after sinus surgery reported smaller or fewer recurrent polyps and improved obstruction scores when mixed-spectrum rhinophototherapy was added to intranasal steroid. Its design does not isolate the light effect.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Nasal polyposis category contains one prospective multicentre human study. Although the source database labels the record randomized, the primary article describes an open study and does not establish random allocation. The intervention was mixed ultraviolet-visible rhinophototherapy added to medication, rather than conventional red or near-infrared PBM alone.

Human and clinical evidence

Kiricsi et al. followed 30 participants after endoscopic sinus surgery. The study compared intranasal corticosteroid alone with corticosteroid plus mUV-VIS rhinophototherapy. Over 12 weeks, with follow-up to 12 months, the authors reported less recurrence or smaller recurrent polyps and better nasal-obstruction scores in the combined-treatment group (2021). Because the study was open and the light was added to steroid treatment, expectation effects and co-intervention prevent a clear causal estimate for light. The small sample also limits confidence in recurrence estimates.

Animal evidence

No animal evidence was identified in the exact category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo evidence was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The reported treatment was mixed polychromatic light spanning 280–650 nm, with ultraviolet and visible components, applied after surgery alongside intranasal steroid. This spectrum is not interchangeable with red or near-infrared PBM. Postoperative surgery and ongoing medication also shape recurrence risk. The study’s open design, small sample, and one centre’s treatment conditions limit transfer to other devices and care settings.

Interpretation

The publication suggests a possible adjunctive effect but cannot separate light from medication, and its primary design description conflicts with the database’s randomized label. It provides very low-certainty evidence for conventional PBM.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for preventing postoperative nasal-polyp recurrence
Publications and records1 human prospective open controlled study.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small open controlled study reported less recurrence and obstruction with ultraviolet-visible rhinophototherapy plus intranasal steroid than steroid alone, but treatment was combined and allocation was not described as randomized in the primary report. The database labels it randomized. Replication should use concealed allocation, sham light, standardized surgery and medication, and longer objective follow-up.

Publication and study types

  • The database labels it randomized, but the primary article describes an open study without confirmed random allocation.
  • No animal or standalone in-vitro evidence.
  • The intervention combined mixed UV-visible rhinophototherapy with intranasal steroid.
